question_en: Of the following investments, the one that most likely offers the greatest protection against contraction risk is a:
option_c: support tranche of a planned amortization class security.
explanation_en: A commercial mortgage–backed security (CMBS) is created from pooled commercial mortgages. Normally, investors in mortgage-backed securities can be exposed to prepayment risk, particularly contraction risk (ie, higher-than-expected prepayments cause the security to be paid off faster than expected). Unlike residential mortgages, commercial mortgages usually restrict prepayments. This means that investors in CMBS have little exposure to contraction risk. (Choice B) A residential mortgage pass-through has one class of bonds, therefore all investors receive scheduled principal payments as well as prepayments. Residential mortgages typically allow borrowers to prepay, so contraction risk is high for these securities. (Choice C) A planned amortization class (PAC) offers limited protection against contraction risk. However, if prepayment rates are higher than anticipated, then PACs will expose investors to contraction risk. The support tranches of these securities assume that risk.

question_en: An analyst finds that a mortgage pass-through security issued three years ago has a prepayment rate of 200 PSA. The analyst's most appropriate conclusion is that the:
option_b: prepayment assumption is half the PSA benchmark.
option_c: collateral had many mortgages at above-market rates.
explanation_en: The Public Securities Association (PSA) created a prepayment model for mortgage-backed securities that has become the benchmark for expressing prepayment rates. The standard model begins with the assumption that borrowers prepay their mortgages at a rate that increases by 0.2% per month for the first 30 months, at which time the rate reaches 6% (ie, 0.2% × 30). Then, prepayments stabilize at a constant 6% rate until the bond is retired. A mortgage-backed security with a value of 100 PSA assumes prepayments fit the standard model. A value of 50 PSA assumes prepayments occur at half the rate of the standard model, and a 200 PSA assumes twice the rate of prepayments (Choice B). If prepayments were assumed to be double the benchmark (200 PSA), the underlying mortgage collateral must have had much higher mortgage rates than the current market environment, as many homeowners were incentivized to refinance their mortgages at lower rates. (Choice A) A 2% prepayment assumption would imply a 33 PSA (ie, 33% of 6%).

question_en: A corporate bond with a 6% annual coupon rate, paid monthly, is quoted at a 5.5% YTM. If the YTM is restated as a bond with semiannual payments, the restated YTM is closest to:
explanation_en: Strategic default: residential mortgages Borrower has sufficient resources to pay but chooses to default Most often occurs with underwater mortgages Most prevalent with nonrecourse loans Has negative credit consequences for the borrower If a borrower defaults on a collateralized loan, such as a conventional residential mortgage, the lender can foreclose (ie, take possession of the collateral and sell it to obtain payment for the loan). Strategic default occurs when a borrower has sufficient resources to pay the mortgage but chooses to default. An underwater mortgage happens when the value of the property is less than the remaining loan balance of the mortgage. Strategic defaults occur most often in underwater mortgages with nonrecourse loans, as the lender has claim only to the proceeds from the sale of the property. In contrast, with a recourse loan, the lender can seize other assets from the borrower if the proceeds from selling the property are insufficient to fully repay the loan, a practice that discourages strategic defaults. For RMBS bondholders, strategic defaults pose two main risks, potential loss of principal and extension risk, since the anticipated maturity of the RMBS increases due to slower prepayments. This is in contrast to contraction risk, which occurs when prepayments accelerate and reduce the expected maturity of the RMBS (Choice A). (Choice B) Interest rate risk refers to the change in the value of a bond that results from interest rate volatility.

question_en: In a nonagency residential mortgage-backed security (RMBS) where a significant portion of the securitized mortgages are nonrecourse and underwater, bondholders are most likely exposed to:
explanation_en: Asset-backed securities (ABS) are bonds that are created by bundling cash-generating loans, such as mortgages. Fixed-rate residential mortgages are often structured as amortizing loans, for which each scheduled payment includes both interest and principal. In theory, residential mortgage–backed securities' (RMBS) maturity coincides with the average maturity of the underlying mortgages; however, the maturity is impacted by prepayments made by the borrowers. Prepayments are often related to changes in interest rates. When rates fall, borrowers are more likely to prepay since they can refinance the loans at a lower rate. This type of prepayment risk is known as contraction risk since it reduces (ie, contracts) the maturity of the RMBS (Choice C). However, when interest rates rise, borrowers are less likely to prepay since their existing mortgage rate is now cheaper by comparison. Fewer prepayments increases the anticipated maturity of the RMBS, which is known as extension risk. (Choice A) Default risk refers to the possibility that borrowers default on the underlying loans. Prepayments are not a default.

question_en: A convertible mortgage is a loan that is best described as one that the borrower can convert from a(n):
explanation_en:
A mortgage is a loan that is collateralized by specific real property, such as a house. If the borrower defaults on the loan, the lender may be
able to seize and sell the property to satisfy the loan amount.
Mortgages can be structured in different ways with respect to their interest rates. A convertible mortgage begins as either a fixed- or variable-rate
loan for a predetermined period (eg, five years). At the end of the initial period, the borrower has the option to change the loan to a variable-rate
loan (if initially a fixed-rate loan) or a fixed-rate loan (if initially a variable-rate loan). "Convertibility" refers only to changing the interest rate
structure, not other characteristics such as amortization or foreclosure rights.
(Choice A) Recourse and nonrecourse refer to the lender's rights if the borrower defaults (ie, foreclosure). A recourse loan allows the lender to
assert claims against the borrower's other assets if the collateral is insufficient to satisfy the loan. A nonrecourse loan permits the lender to look
only to the collateral to satisfy the loan.
(Choice B) Amortization refers to how a mortgage loan's principal is paid. A convertible loan refers only to the borrower's option to change the
loan from one type of interest rate to another, not how the loan is amortized.

subtopic: 8.01 Derivative Instrument and Derivative Market Features
question_en: An advantage to an investor using the over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives market rather than an exchange is most likely:
explanation_en: Over-the-counter (OTC) trading occurs directly between two parties who are free to negotiate any terms of the trade. Trades made on an exchange do not allow such flexibility since contracts offered by an exchange have standardized terms that participants cannot alter. (Choice A) OTC trades are less regulated than trades on exchanges. OTC participants typically have few, if any, disclosure requirements concerning their trades. In contrast, all trades made on an exchange are publicly available and participants have no expectation that their activity will be private. (Choice C) Trading through an exchange eliminates counterparty risk, which is the risk that the other party will fail to perform as obligated (ie, default). Counterparty risk is always present with bilateral OTC trades.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\8. Derivatives\8.01 Derivative Instrument and Derivative Market Features - Answers.pdf
subtopic: 8.01 Derivative Instrument and Derivative Market Features
question_en: Which of the following is most likely an advantage of over-the-counter derivatives compared to similar exchange-traded contracts?
explanation_en: Derivatives are traded both on exchanges and in the over-the-counter (OTC) market. Where the contracts are traded affects how the terms of the contracts are determined. Exchange-traded derivatives have standardized terms set by the exchange where they are traded. OTC contracts are negotiated by the buyer and seller. Exchange-traded contracts specify the quantity and quality of the underlying (eg, 1,000 barrels of light sweet crude oil), delivered to a specific location (eg, Cushing, Oklahoma). For a commercial user or producer dealing in a different grade (eg, heavy sour crude oil) or wanting to make or take delivery in a different location (eg, Southeast Asia), standardized contracts may not be optimal risk management tools. Since OTC contracts are negotiated by the counterparties, their terms can be customized to address specific risk management goals. (Choice A) Although OTC derivative markets are coming under increased regulatory scrutiny, exchange-traded derivatives are subject to significantly greater regulatory oversight. (Choice B) The exchange functions as a clearinghouse, effectively eliminating counterparty credit risk from exchange-traded contracts. OTC contracts have no guarantor, so each counterparty is exposed to the other's credit risk.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\8. Derivatives\8.01 Derivative Instrument and Derivative Market Features - Answers.pdf
subtopic: 8.01 Derivative Instrument and Derivative Market Features
question_en: Which of the following is most likely an advantage of exchange-traded derivatives compared to similar over-the-counter contracts?
explanation_en: Derivatives are traded on exchanges or in the over-the-counter (OTC) market. Where and how they are traded creates important differences between exchange-traded versus OTC derivatives related to contract terms and counterparty credit risk. Contract terms: Exchange-traded derivatives have standardized terms set by the exchange on which they are traded. OTC contract terms are negotiated by the buyer and seller. Legal counterparty: All derivative contracts are created by a trade between two parties. OTC derivatives remain bilateral contracts between the initial buyer and seller whereas the clearinghouse becomes the counterparty to all exchange-traded derivatives after contract creation. By becoming a party to all exchange-traded contracts, the clearinghouse is positioned to guarantee performance. Since clearinghouses are well- funded financial institutions, they do provide guarantees and thus effectively remove counterparty credit risk from exchange-traded contracts. OTC contracts do not have a third-party guarantor, so both counterparties are exposed to the other's credit risk. (Choice A) Both OTC and exchange-traded derivatives are used for similar risk management strategies such as hedging asset price risk or locking in an exchange rate for a future currency trade. (Choice C) Exchange-traded derivative contract terms are fixed by the exchange (ie, standardized). Since OTC contracts are negotiated by the counterparties, the terms can be customized to address market participants' specific risk management needs.

subtopic: 8.01 Derivative Instrument and Derivative Market Features
question_en: For otherwise equivalent futures and forward contracts, there is most likely a difference in the:
option_a: timing of their gains and losses.
option_c: approximate amount of their gains and losses.
explanation_en: Futures vs. forwards: similarities and differences Futures Forwards Contractual obligations Long obligated to buy and short obligated to sell at expiration Contract pricing = Spot price [1 + (net cost of carry)]Time to expiration Contract terms Standardized Negotiated Legal counterparty Clearinghouse Trade counterparty Gain/loss realization Settled daily in cash Settled at expiration Futures and forward contracts have some similar features but also several distinct differences. Both are derivatives that place the same obligations on their contract counterparties. Also, futures and forward prices both reflect arbitrage pricing. Futures and forwards differ in several respects. Determination of contract terms: Forward contract terms are negotiated by the buyer and seller. Futures contract terms are standardized by the exchange where the contracts are traded. Legal counterparty: Forwards are bilateral contracts between the original buyer and seller, whereas futures trades involve a clearinghouse that functions as the counterparty to both the buyer and the seller. Timing of gains and losses: Forward contract gains and losses are settled at expiration. Futures gains and losses are realized daily through mark-to-market valuation. (Choice B) Futures and forwards impose the same obligation on their respective counterparties. Both require the long party to buy and the short party to sell the underlying asset at expiration. (Choice C) Futures and forward prices on otherwise equivalent contracts are usually the same since they are based on the same arbitrage- pricing relationship. Consequently, futures and forwards almost always result in approximately the same amount of gains and losses.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\8. Derivatives\8.01 Derivative Instrument and Derivative Market Features - Answers.pdf
subtopic: 8.01 Derivative Instrument and Derivative Market Features
question_en: The source of return for a derivatives dealer in the over-the-counter market is least likely to be:
option_b: dealer transactions at the bid-ask spread.
option_c: gains on the derivative caused by gains in the underlying.
explanation_en: Dealers in the over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives market act as the counterparty for participants who want to buy or sell derivatives. Dealers provide liquidity by quoting what they will pay for a derivative (ie, bid price) and a price to sell the same derivative (ie, ask price). The ask price is higher than the bid price and the spread is the difference between the ask and bid prices. Dealers may try to maintain a "flat" position (ie, long positions netted against short positions). If successful, their return consists of the spread between the bid and ask prices. However, market conditions can force dealers into a net long or short position, which exposes them to risk. Their assumption of risk distinguishes them from brokers, who facilitate transactions between two parties. Brokers do not hold positions, so they do not assume any risk. Brokers earn a commission for their services, but a dealer's spread is not a commission (Choice B). Dealers can also earn returns from intentionally taking on risk by establishing a long or short derivative position. This would occur if they believe that the price of the underlying will move favorably, which makes the derivative more valuable (Choice C).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\8. Derivatives\8.01 Derivative Instrument and Derivative Market Features - Answers.pdf
subtopic: 8.01 Derivative Instrument and Derivative Market Features
question_en: Compared with over-the-counter derivatives, derivatives traded on an exchange are least likely to be characterized by:
explanation_en: Derivatives can be traded on an exchange, which acts as a central counterparty for buyers and sellers of different types of futures contracts and options. This eliminates counterparty risk (ie, the risk that the other party to a contract will default). This is significantly different from derivatives traded "over-the-counter" (OTC), which are bilateral agreements (ie, directly between two parties). OTC contracts have little regulatory oversight since most participants in the OTC market are large institutions that can evaluate the risks of both the contract and the counterparty. Exchanges attract a wide range of participants, including less sophisticated investors. Regulations are designed in part to provide assurance that institutional investors do not have an unfair advantage (Choice A). To better facilitate its role as the only counterparty, as well as to provide liquidity, an exchange imposes a high degree of standardization on the contracts traded on the exchange. Terms such as dates, quantities, and delivery specifications are identical for all traders in a given contract. In contrast, parties to OTC contracts can negotiate all the terms of the contract (Choice B).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\8. Derivatives\8.01 Derivative Instrument and Derivative Market Features - Answers.pdf
subtopic: 8.01 Derivative Instrument and Derivative Market Features
question_en: The amount due for a plain vanilla interest rate swap payment is most likely based on the interest rates of each payment stream and the swap's:
explanation_en: Most interest rate swaps obligate the counterparties to periodically exchange a series of fixed and floating payments; in practice, only the net difference of those payments is exchanged. Such fixed-for-floating swaps are so common that they are referred to as plain vanilla swaps. The fixed payments are based on an interest rate set at the contract's inception. The floating payments are based on a reference rate that resets at the beginning of each payment period. The amount due from each counterparty equals the interest rate each is obligated to pay multiplied by the notional principal of the swap. The notional principal is similar to a bond's par value in that both are used to determine the payment amount implied by a specific interest rate. However, unlike a bond's par value, which represents an amount borrowed that must be repaid, the notional principal is never transferred between the counterparties, so it is never repaid (Choice A). (Choice B) A swap's market value is the amount one counterparty is obligated to pay the other to terminate a swap prior to expiration. A swap's market value is not used to determine the payment amounts due on a swap payment date.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\8. Derivatives\8.02 Forward Commitment and Contingent Claim Features and Instruments - Answers.pdf
subtopic: 8.02 Forward Commitment and Contingent Claim Features and Instruments
question_en: Which of the following forward commitments is least likely to expose investors to default?
explanation_en: In both forward and futures contracts, counterparties agree to buy or sell an underlying asset at a fixed price at expiration. Swap counterparties agree to exchange a series of cash payments, usually based on streams of fixed and floating payments that reflect the value of some underlying asset. Exposure to credit risk and loss in the event of default depends on the legal counterparty to the contract. That counterparty is primarily determined by where and how the contract is traded. Futures contracts are always traded on exchanges. After a trade is executed between a buyer and seller, the exchange's clearinghouse becomes the legal counterparty to each side of the contract. Forwards and swaps trade over the counter (OTC). A significant number of these contracts are bilateral, and the counterparties in the original trade remain the legal counterparties. By becoming a party to all exchange-traded contracts, the clearinghouse is positioned to guarantee performance to the counterparties. Clearinghouses are well-funded financial institutions, so their guarantees minimize investors' exposure to default on futures contracts. OTC contracts (eg, swaps, forwards) lack third-party guarantors, so they expose their counterparties to default risk (Choices A and C).

question_en: If the credit protection buyer of a credit default swap (CDS) chooses a cash settlement after a credit event, the required payment from the credit protection seller is most likely:
option_a: established by an auction after the credit event.
option_b: negotiated between the counterparties after the credit event.
option_c: a preset amount of money established at the creation of the CDS.
explanation_en: Credit default swaps (CDS): credit event settlements Description Money amount Cash Credit protection seller pays credit protection buyer restitution for Settlement payment determined through an auction settlement decline in value of securities of defaulted securities Physical Buyer of credit protection turns over insured securities and Amount of payment determined at CDS creation delivery receives a fixed amount of money Credit default swaps (CDS) are contingent claim derivative contracts that insure against credit losses on third-party debt instruments. Credit protection buyers make a series of payments to credit protection sellers over the life of the CDS. Credit protection sellers make a cash settlement payment to buyers only if a credit event occurs. The most common type of settlement resulting from a credit event is a cash settlement. After a credit event, the value of the insured securities is determined at auction. Credit protection sellers must pay credit protection buyers cash equal to the difference between the value determined at auction and the amount of insurance protection purchased by the buyer (ie, defaulted amount). (Choice B) Negotiation is not used to determine the settlement payments on a CDS. (Choice C) If physical delivery is the chosen method for settlement of a credit event, the credit protection buyer receives a preset amount of money (ie, full insured amount) in return for delivering the defaulted securities to the credit protection seller.

subtopic: 8.02 Forward Commitment and Contingent Claim Features and Instruments
question_en: An investor sells a European call for GBP 3 with a strike price of GBP 50. Based only on this information, which of the following best describes the investor's loss potential?
explanation_en: A European call option gives its buyer (ie, long call) the right—but not the obligation—to purchase an underlying asset at the exercise price (ie, strike price) on the date of expiration. The option seller (ie, short call) sells this right and collects a premium (ie, price of the option contract). The seller will be forced to sell the stock to the buyer at the strike price if the call is exercised. If at expiration the price of the stock is less than the exercise price, the option will expire with no value and the seller's profit is the option premium. The premium received is always the maximum profit for a seller of an option contract. (S ) (X) If at expiration the price of the stock T is greater than the exercise price , the buyer will exercise the option and the seller's profit will be the option premium less the difference between the exercise price and the stock price. Potential losses for a short call position are considered unlimited since there is no limit on the price of the underlying stock. (Choice B) If the investor had purchased (ie, been in the long call position), the maximum potential loss would have been the premium paid (in this scenario, GBP 3). (Choice C) A short put position would result in a maximum potential loss of GBP 47 (eg, 3 − 50) if the underlying stock fell to zero.

subtopic: 8.02 Forward Commitment and Contingent Claim Features and Instruments
question_en: Which of the following factors least likely contributes to the liquidity of futures contracts?
explanation_en: Features of futures contracts Contractual Short (long) party obligated to sell (buy) commitments underlying asset Exchange traded No over-the-counter trading of futures Clearinghouse Exchange clearinghouse as legal counterparty Standardized Exchange sets all contract terms contracts Margin requirements Cash deposits to cover losses on positions Gains and losses on open positions realized in Daily settlement cash daily Allowable price change from previous day's Daily price limits settlement price Features that enhance the liquidity of futures trading include the following: The clearinghouse becomes the legal counterparty to both the original buyer and the original seller of the contract. All contracts on a given underlying asset for a specific expiration have identical, standardized terms. Futures positions are usually offset by creating the opposite position (eg, taking a short position to offset a long position). Offsetting does not require transacting with the original counterparty, and since traders can use standardized contracts, there is a large universe of potential buyers and sellers. The lack of a direct contractual link between the original buyer and the original seller and the uniformity of contract terms contribute to the liquidity of futures (Choices B and C). Daily price limits determine the range of prices at which futures can trade. Price limits are designed to limit the clearinghouse's credit risk exposure by capping traders' losses in any trading session. Price limits can restrict liquidity by preventing trades when buyers and sellers want to trade at prices outside of the limited range.

question_en:
A trader takes a long stock futures position and deposits the initial margin requirement in cash under the following circumstances:

| Selected Maintenance margin | Data (in €) 6 |
|---|---|
| Futures price | 150 |
| Initial margin | 15 |

If the next futures settlement price is €140, the amount of the margin call issued to the trader is closest to:
explanation_en: Traders must meet an initial margin requirement in cash when initiating a futures position. To ensure there are adequate funds to cover losses, the margin account value must be maintained above a minimum amount known as the maintenance margin. If the account value falls below the maintenance margin, there is a demand for additional funds, which is referred to as a margin call. The amount of the margin call is the cash necessary to raise the account value to the initial margin requirement. The €10 price decline results in an equal loss on the long futures position (ie, -150 + 140 = −10), which reduces the account value to €5 (15 −10). The margin call is for the difference between the account value and the initial margin, €10 = 15 − 5. Failure to meet the call in full can result in a liquidation of positions. (Choice A) €1 is the shortfall of the account value relative to the maintenance margin. A margin call that brings the account equity back up to the maintenance margin is a requirement in the securities market, not the futures market. (Choice B) A deposit of €9 would raise the account value to €14, equal to 10% of the current cash value of the futures contract. However, futures margins are expressed as a specific money amount per contract, not as a percentage of a contract's cash value.

subtopic: 8.02 Forward Commitment and Contingent Claim Features and Instruments
question_en: A European put option with an exercise price of €85 is selling for €5. At expiration, if the put seller's profit for the short position is €2, then the underlying spot price is closest to:
explanation_en: A European put option gives its buyer the right, but not the obligation, to sell an underlying asset (ie, underlying) at the exercise price on the expiration date. The put writer (ie, short) is obligated to buy the underlying from the put buyer (ie, long) upon exercise. In exchange for this right, the long pays the short an initial premium, which represents the maximum possible profit to the short. At expiration, the short position's payoff and profit equals the negative of the long position's payoff and profit. In this scenario, the short party received an initial premium of €5. The short's profit (€2) is the premium plus the short's payoff at expiration; therefore, the short's payoff at expiration must be €−3. This results when the spot price is €82 since the short is obligated to buy the underlying at the higher exercise price of €85. (Choice A) €78 results in a profit of €2 for the long, not the short. (Choice C) €88 results in a €2 profit for a short call, not a short put, position.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\8. Derivatives\8.02 Forward Commitment and Contingent Claim Features and Instruments - Answers.pdf
subtopic: 8.02 Forward Commitment and Contingent Claim Features and Instruments
question_en: On the day of expiration, a European call option with an exercise price of USD 50 has an underlying asset with a value of USD 57. If USD 2 was paid to purchase the option, the call buyer's profit is closest to:
explanation_en: A European call option gives its holder the right, but not the obligation, to buy an underlying asset at the exercise price on the date of expiration. The asset can then be sold at the market price. If the market price is greater than the exercise price, then the call buyer will exercise the option. The difference between the exercise price and the market price is the call buyer's payoff. If the market price is not higher than the exercise price, then the call buyer will not exercise it and there will be no payoff. So, the call buyer's payoff is the greater of (market price – exercise price) and zero. The call buyer's profit equals the payoff minus the amount the buyer paid to purchase the option: In this scenario, the call buyer paid USD 2 for the option; the exercise price is USD 50, and the value of the underlying is USD 57. The payoff is (57 – 50) = USD 7, and the profit is (7 – 2) = USD 5. (Choice A) USD −7 is the result of subtracting the market price from the exercise price, and then failing to account for the cost of the option. (Choice C) USD 7 is the payoff of the call buyer in this scenario. The payoff does not include the cost of the option to the call buyer (USD 2).
